chunks: From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qassani, from a man whose name he mentioned, from Abdullah ibn al-Qasim al-Ja'fari, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

The world longed for a group whose wealth was purely permissible, but they did not desire it, so they passed by. Then it longed for a group whose wealth was permissible mixed with doubt, so they said, 'We have no need of the doubt,' and expanded in the permissible. Then it longed for a group whose wealth was forbidden mixed with doubt, so they said, 'We have no need of the forbidden,' and expanded in the doubt. Then it longed for a group whose wealth was purely forbidden, so they sought it but did not find it. And the believer eats in the world with the status of the one in need (of sustenance).

And Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar wrote to Abu Muhammad (peace be upon him): A man bought an estate or a servant with money he took from banditry or from theft. Is it permissible for him to consume what enters him from the fruit of this estate? Or is it permissible for him to have intercourse with this private part which he bought from theft or from banditry? He (peace be upon him) wrote: 'There is no good in anything whose origin is forbidden, and its use is not permissible.'

key_terms.الْمُضْطَرِّ: The one in need / the one who eats out of necessity

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on using property or servants bought with illicit money in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from Al-Kafi, transmitted through the chain of Al-Qasani, illustrates the spiritual hierarchy of believers in their engagement with the world, culminating in the concept of the 'mukhtār' (one who chooses) who consumes worldly goods with the caution of the 'muḍṭar' (one in necessity). It is paired with a legal ruling from Imam al-Hadi (AS) via Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, establishing that the fruit of illicitly acquired property remains impermissible due to the impurity of its origin, a principle central to Shia jurisprudence on 'ghaṣb' and 'kharāj'.
